messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kai remembers the night his father came home smelling of beer, the way the front door slammed hard enough to rattle the pictures in the hallway. He was six, maybe seven, standing at the top of the stairs in his pajamas, watching his mother shrink against the kitchen counter. The memory arrives in disconnected pieces—the glint of a broken glass, the sound of his mother's voice saying "please, not tonight," the heavy thud of a fist against the wall beside her head. He can never see the whole picture, only fragments that feel like they belong to someone else's life, and yet when they surface they bring back the same raw terror he felt as a child, his heart slamming against his ribs as if he were still standing on those stairs.

Now eighteen and working as a project manager for a small construction firm, Kai has learned to navigate a world that feels full of hidden threats. He watches other people closely for signs that they might harm him, scanning their faces for the subtle shift that precedes violence. The smell of alcohol on a colleague's breath at a team meeting is enough to make his hands tremble and his mind go blank, and he finds himself suddenly unable to remember the safety briefing he was about to deliver. That olfactory trigger sends him straight to the memory fragments, and the memory fragments in turn make every man he encounters feel like a potential danger.

Kai has developed routines that keep the world manageable. He avoids other people as much as his job allows, eating lunch alone in his car and leaving the office the moment his shift ends. When he cannot avoid being alone with male coworkers, he keeps his back to the wall and his eyes on the door, checking the locks repeatedly even though he knows they are secure. He jumps at ordinary sounds—the hiss of a radiator, the clatter of a dropped tool—and each startle response sends a fresh wave of fragmented memory crashing through his mind, which only makes him watch the men around him more closely.

He drinks most evenings, sometimes heavily, and smokes cigarettes to steady his nerves during the day. The alcohol dulls the edges of the memories, but it also makes him more vigilant the next morning, more certain that something bad is coming. He has come to believe that if he stops checking the locks, if he stops watching the men around him, the violence he witnessed as a child will find him again. His girlfriend has started to notice that he flinches when she touches his shoulder from behind, and that he never rides his bicycle anymore—not since the day a car backfired on the bike path and he nearly swerved into traffic, the sound triggering a cascade of fragmented images that left him shaking on the grass for twenty minutes.

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment at work last week. A new hire, a large man with a friendly manner, offered Kai a ride home. The smell of the man's cologne mixed with something faintly alcoholic, and Kai froze in the parking lot, unable to speak, his mind flooded with images of his father's hands and his mother's face. He walked home instead, four miles in the dark, checking over his shoulder every few steps. He is afraid that he is losing control, that the world is closing in around him. But what frightens him most is the thought that if he stops being afraid, if he stops watching and checking and avoiding, he will be caught off guard the way his mother was—and that next time, it will be him who becomes the danger.
